fetched_contents.text: Evidence-Based Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training on Exercise Capacity and Health: A Review with Historical Perspective Abstract Engaging in regular exercise results in a range of physiological adaptations offering benefits for exercise capacity and health, independent of age, gender or the presence of chronic diseases. Accumulating evidence shows that lack of time is a major impediment to exercise, causing physical inactivity worldwide. This issue has resulted in momentum for interval training models known to elicit higher enjoyment and induce adaptations similar to or greater than moderate-intensity continuous training, despite a lower total exercise volume. Although there is no universal definition, high-intensity interval exercise is characterized by repeated short bursts of intense activity, performed with a “near maximal” or “all-out” effort corresponding to ≥90% of maximal oxygen uptake or >75% of maximal power, with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise. Research has indicated that high-intensity interval training induces numerous physiological adaptations that improve exercise capacity (maximal oxygen uptake, aerobic endurance, anaerobic capacity etc.) and metabolic health in both clinical and healthy (athletes, active and inactive individuals without any apparent disease or disorder) populations. In this paper, a brief history of high-intensity interval training is presented, based on the novel findings of some selected studies on exercise capacity and health, starting from the early 1920s to date. Further, an overview of the mechanisms underlying the physiological adaptations in response to high-intensity interval training is provided. Keywords: exercise, intermittent training, physical endurance, health benefits, physiological adaptation 1. Introduction Exercise is a cornerstone in the primary prevention of chronic diseases including diabetes mellitus, cancer, obesity, hypertension, coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, and depression [1,2,3]. For centuries, exercise has long been prescribed by physicians as a medicine for their patients [4], and quotes attributed to Hippocrates, the father of Western medicine, include: “Walking is man’s best medicine” and “if there is a deficiency in food and exercise, the body will fall sick [5,6].” Evidence-based scientific guidelines suggest that exercise is a novel non-pharmacological strategy in the prevention and management of chronic diseases [7,8,9,10,11]. Despite these well-documented benefits of exercise, a third of adults and four-fifths of adolescents—approximately 1.4 billion people—do not meet public health guidelines for recommended levels of exercise [7], making physical inactivity a global problem [12]. The recently updated World Health Organization 2020 Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behavior [13] recommend performing at least 150 to 300 min of moderate-intensity physical activity, or 75 to 150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise, per week to achieve substantial health benefits [14]. However, the lack of sufficient time is the most common barrier to adhering to regular exercise [15]. Therefore, research has recently focused on interval training models, which consist of brief periods of intense activity performed with a “near-maximal” or “all-out” effort corresponding to ≥90 of maximal oxygen uptake (V˙O2max) [16] or >75% of maximal power [17], interspersed with passive or active recovery periods, that can induce similar or even greater physiological adaptations when compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) [17,18,19], which generally consists of 30–60 min of moderate-intensity exercise at 40% to <60% of oxygen consumption reserve [20,21]. There are numerous excellent reviews on the effects of interval training on exercise capacity and general health in healthy and clinic populations as well as the mechanisms underlying these effects [15,18,22,23,24]. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study to date has applied a historical approach. In this review, after defining the types of different interval-training models, the findings of some selected high-intensity interval-training studies that have received considerable interest due to their novel findings on exercise capacity and health, which can be considered milestone studies in the related literature, are presented. Finally, a brief overview of the mechanisms underlying the physiological adaptations in response to high-intensity interval training is presented. 2. Interval Training Interval training is characterized by short bursts of intense activities that elicit ≥90% of V˙O2max [16], >75% of maximal power [17] or supra-maximal effort [16,17,18], with periods of rest or low-intensity exercise for recovery. The most used types of interval training models are: (1) the high-intensity interval training (HIIT) model with submaximal efforts that elicit ≥90% of V˙O2max [16] or >75% of maximal power [18,25]; (2) the sprint interval training (SIT) model, a more intense version of HIIT that involves maximal or supramaximal efforts greater than V˙O2max or maximal power; and (3) the repeated-sprint training (RST) model, which is characterized by performing a high number of sprints lasting less than 10 s interspersed with relatively shorter recoveries (<60 s) compared to the recovery periods of SIT [26]. Interval training has been an integral part of training for coaches and athletes to enhance performance for over a century, and it has received considerable scientific inquiry due to its ability to induce remarkable physiological adaptations and health benefits that resemble MICT with less time commitment [27]. Introduction Obesity is defined as excessive accumulation of body fat1 that is strongly associated with several harmful health conditions2 such as insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, atherosclerosis, systemic arterial hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, stroke, among others.3,4 In Brazil, it has been estimated in 2021 that excess weight affected 57.2% of the population and the obesity prevalence was 22.4%.5 Excess body fat—body and/or abdominal visceral fat assessed as total mass or percentage—is a major health concern as people engage in sedentary lifestyles. There is no consensus on the gold standard for body composition. However, dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) provides accurate measures of bone mineral content, body fat mass, lean mass and visceral fat in limb or whole-body assessments.6 It is thus currently the reference method for body composition assessment and is used to validate predictive equations for doubly indirect methods.7, 8, 9, 10 Several research studies have investigated the relationship between exercise training and weight reduction in individuals with obesity.11,12 Traditional aerobic exercises involving continuous aerobic training (CAT, moderate-intensity exercise ranges between 40% and 60–65% of maximal VO2 max) and/or resistance exercise can have beneficial effects and improve body composition by reducing body fat mass and increasing lean mass.13,14 However, other exercise modalities, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), appear to produce at least similar beneficial effects on body composition as traditional aerobic exercises.15 There is no universal definition of HIIT. Typically, it is characterized by short bursts of high-intensity activity interspersed by periods of (active or passive) rest with the advantage of a shorter time frame and total session duration over CAT. The American College of Sports Medicine states that for high-intensity exercise is above 65% of maximal VO2 max.14 However, intensity below 80% of maximal VO2 max, we should not consider generally this as high-intensity training.16 HIIT mostly involves greater energy expenditure than CAT (of moderate intensity and volume). It is thus logical to believe that greater energy expenditure would result in greater reduction of body fat. This is further supported by a greater effect of HIIT on VO2 max17 as well as the effect of excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC)18 compared to CAT. These adaptations would be associated with fatty acid oxidation, thereby contributing to body fat reduction. Some evidence suggests that HIIT offers significant benefits in reducing body fat,19, 20, 21 but other studies have not shown these same benefits.22, 23, 24, 25 A number of meta-analyses have aimed to further examine these effects, but they involved different populations26,27 or different body composition assessment methods27,28 as well as other factors that may affect the results. fetched_contents.text: HIIT Workout Plan: Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced Exercises to Try Following a HIIT workout plan is one way to see some serious fitness gains in a short amount of time. This workout method mixes fast, intense bursts of exercise with brief recovery periods to give you a full workout without the need to log hours in the gym. HIIT can realistically contribute to weight loss, but the evidence suggests it is not a standalone miracle solution and should be viewed in the context of overall energy balance, recovery, and individual physiology.

## How much fat or weight HIIT burns in a session
The evidence supports the idea that HIIT is high-intensity and burns calories both during and after exercise, but it does not provide a precise, universally applicable number of calories burned per session for weight loss. The HIIT physiology review notes that HIIT induces numerous physiological adaptations that improve exercise capacity and metabolic health, including increases in maximal oxygen uptake and aerobic endurance [N1-F1]. Healthline similarly states that HIIT can boost metabolism for hours after exercise, resulting in burning additional calories even after the workout [N1-R2]. The practical HIIT plan example also emphasizes that HIIT mixes fast, intense bursts with brief recovery periods and “burns more calories during and after your workout” [N4-F4]. However, the evidence does not give a specific session-level calorie burn figure for fat loss, and this is important because calorie expenditure depends on individual factors such as body weight, intensity, duration, and the specific exercises used.

## How HIIT compares to steady-state cardio for weight loss
The evidence indicates that HIIT may offer some advantages over steady-state cardio, but the weight-loss comparison is not straightforward. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that aerobic exercise at least 150 minutes per week was associated with clinically important reductions in waist circumference and measures of body fat [N2-R1]. Another study on high-intensity intermittent exercise and fat loss notes that brief HIIE interventions (2 to 6 weeks) only resulted in negligible weight loss, suggesting that duration and program design matter [N2-R2]. A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis found that HIIT is not superior to continuous aerobic training in reducing body fat or abdominal visceral fat in individuals with excess weight [N2-F3]. It also found that HIIT may offer at least similar beneficial effects on body composition as traditional aerobic exercise, but the evidence is mixed and influenced by population differences, body composition assessment methods, and other factors [N2-F3]. A comparative study of HIIT versus moderate continuous training found both methods had positive effects on aerobic capacity, fat oxidation, and other metabolic outcomes [N2-R3]. Overall, HIIT appears to be a time-efficient and metabolically stimulating option, but steady-state cardio may still have a more consistent and reproducible weight-loss effect in many people [N2-R1][N2-F3].

## Why diet and total energy deficit matter more than exercise alone
The evidence is clear that exercise alone is unlikely to produce substantial weight loss without dietary changes. The nutrition and lifestyle search results emphasize that small, balanced meals throughout the day help keep energy levels steady, and that nutrition supports sleep and exercise [N5-R1]. Sleep, stress, and weight-loss guidance also state that impaired sleep throws hunger levels, metabolism, and energy levels out of balance [N5-R2]. The energy balance dynamics review states that physical activity and diet interventions can yield modest weight loss and that combined interventions have synergistic effects that promote sustained weight loss [N5-R3]. The effective weight loss strategies source similarly states that when exercise and nutrition work together, they create a synergistic effect that enhances weight loss efforts [N5-R4]. In short, the evidence supports the view that total energy deficit—driven by diet and expenditure—is the dominant determinant of weight loss, while HIIT contributes more through metabolic stimulation, time efficiency, and adaptation than through massive calorie burning alone [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## Bottom line
HIIT can realistically support weight loss by improving metabolism, burning calories during and after exercise, and offering a time-efficient way to accumulate physical activity [N1-R2][N4-F4]. However, it is not superior to steady-state cardio in all weight-loss contexts, and the evidence suggests that brief HIIE programs may yield only modest results [N2-R2][N2-F3]. Diet and total energy deficit remain far more important than exercise alone; without dietary changes and an overall energy deficit, even intense HIIT is unlikely to produce rapid, meaningful weight loss [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## A realistic daily schedule combining HIIT, cardio, strength, and rest
The practical HIIT plan evidence describes a flexible exercise structure that mixes short intense bursts with brief recovery periods, and that can be adapted for beginners, intermediates, and advanced levels [N4-F4]. It also provides specific sample schedules, including a beginner HIIT plan of 15 minutes, an intermediate plan of 20 minutes, and an advanced plan of 30 minutes [N4-F4]. The general HIIT plan source similarly states that HIIT is a way to see serious fitness gains in a short amount of time without needing to log hours in the gym [N4-R1]. For a weight-loss-focused daily plan, a realistic schedule would likely alternate HIIT with moderate cardio and strength training, while preserving rest days.

One plausible daily structure, based on the evidence, is:
- **Morning/Afternoon**: HIIT session (e.g., 15–30 minutes, depending on fitness level)
- **Evening**: Light cardio or strength training (e.g., 20–40 minutes)
- **Rest day**: Full rest or active recovery (e.g., walking, stretching, yoga)
- **Weekly pattern**: 3–4 days of exercise, 1–2 rest days [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4]

The evidence also supports a balanced approach: HIIT is not a one-size-fits-all replacement for all exercise, and a six- to eight-week HIIT plan is presented as a flexible framework for different fitness levels [N4-F4]. The nutrition and lifestyle evidence reinforces that sleep, stress, and nutrition are central to health and performance [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Therefore, the best daily plan should include:
- **HIIT** for time efficiency and metabolic stimulation
- **Cardio** for sustained calorie burning and cardiovascular health
- **Strength training** for preserving lean mass and metabolic rate [N4-F4][N5-R3]
- **Rest and recovery** to avoid overtraining and maintain performance [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4]

## How to adjust intensity, duration, and exercise selection
The evidence supports progressive adjustment over time rather than an all-out, daily-only plan. The beginner HIIT plan uses shorter intervals and longer recovery, while the intermediate plan increases work intervals and shortens rest, and the advanced plan further increases intensity and shortens rest [N4-F4]. The physician’s own explanation also notes that HIIT can be modified for beginners or advanced athletes with changes in interval duration and exercise selection [N1-F1]. The progression guidance sources reinforce this: novice training is 2–3 days per week, intermediate 3–4 days, and advanced 4–5 days [N6-R1]. The 10% rule also suggests that training load should not increase by more than 10% per week [N6-R2].

For a weight-loss plan, intensity should start relatively low and gradually increase, with attention to form and symptoms. The evidence explicitly warns that HIIT is not “halfheartedly” done; you must give it your all during bursts, but also that form is important to avoid injury [N4-F4]. The same source recommends starting with shorter intervals at around 80 percent effort and gradually ramping up [N4-F4]. Exercise selection should vary to keep the program engaging and to target different energy systems, including strength, cardio, and full-body movements [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The practical plan example includes bodyweight squats, push-ups, jumping jacks, mountain climbers, burpees, jump squats, push-up variations, high knees, planks, and burpee with tuck jumps [N4-F4]. For weight loss, the plan should also include sufficient volume and variety to maintain engagement and metabolic adaptation.

## What to eat before, during, and after workouts
The evidence underscores that nutrition and sleep are essential to support performance and recovery. The wellness trio source states that smaller, balanced meals throughout the day help keep energy levels steady [N5-R1]. Sleep and weight-loss guidance notes that impaired sleep throws hunger, metabolism, and energy levels out of balance [N5-R2]. Energy balance dynamics also states that physical activity and diet interventions can yield modest weight loss and that combined interventions have synergistic effects [N5-R3]. Effective weight-loss strategies likewise emphasize that exercise and nutrition together create a synergistic effect [N5-R4]. Therefore, the plan should include pre-workout, during-workout, and post-workout nutrition.

- **Before workouts**: Small, balanced meals or snacks containing carbohydrates and protein can support energy and endurance [N5-R1]. The evidence does not specify exact pre-workout meals, but it implies that steady energy intake helps maintain performance and prevent fatigue [N5-R1][N5-R2].
- **During workouts**: Hydration is important, and the evidence suggests that hydration, nutrition, exercise, and sleep should be optimized together [N5-R5]. While the HIIT plan evidence does not detail intra-workout nutrition, it does emphasize that form, intensity, and recovery are key [N4-F4].
- **After workouts**: Post-workout nutrition should support recovery and muscle repair, with protein and carbohydrates likely important. The evidence does not give a specific post-workout meal formula, but it supports the idea that sleep and nutrition work together to support exercise and weight-loss outcomes [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

## Bottom line
A realistic daily plan for weight loss with HIIT should be balanced, progressive, and recovery-oriented. HIIT can be used as a core component of the week, combined with cardio and strength training, and protected by rest days [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Intensity, duration, and exercise selection should be adjusted gradually, starting at a manageable level and increasing only when tolerated and supported by recovery [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Nutrition and sleep are central to performance and weight loss, so the plan should include balanced meals, hydration, and sufficient rest [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence does not support an extreme daily-only high-intensity plan as a realistic or safe weight-loss strategy.

The evidence is clear that prolonged or repeated high-intensity exercise can have negative effects. This means that daily high-intensity training should not be assumed safe. The evidence also supports the idea that high-intensity training should be progressive and not increased too rapidly [N6-R2].

The overtraining sources emphasize that adequate recovery is necessary to prevent fatigue and declining performance [N3-R3][N3-R2]. In fact, the evidence suggests the opposite: recovery and sleep are essential to maintaining the metabolic and physical capacity needed for effective training and weight loss [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-R2][N5-R3].

The evidence supports reducing intensity or adding rest days when signs of overtraining appear. Overtraining syndrome is treated by stopping high-intensity training sessions [N3-R2]. It also supports the 10% rule, meaning training load should not increase by more than 10% per week [N6-R2]. The periodization and progression evidence further supports a gradual, cyclical approach rather than abrupt increases in intensity [N6-R3][N6-R4].

For a weight-loss plan, the practical recommendation is:
- **Reduce intensity** if fatigue, soreness, or performance decline appears
- **Add rest days** when overtraining symptoms are present or when recovery is insufficient
- **Progress gradually** by increasing load only by small amounts and only when tolerated [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2]

Extreme daily high-intensity training is not supported by the evidence as a safe or realistic approach. Recovery, sleep, and overtraining limits are essential to preserving performance and preventing injury [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The evidence also shows that recovery and sleep are central to maintaining metabolic and exercise capacity, which in turn supports weight loss [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Therefore, the safest and most effective strategy is to train intensely but not excessively, with rest days and progressive adjustments based on recovery and symptoms [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

A realistic daily schedule would combine HIIT with cardio and strength training while preserving rest and recovery. - **Evening**: Light cardio or strength training (e.g., 20–40 minutes)

The evidence supports progressive adjustment over time rather than an all-out, daily-only plan. ## How much fat or weight HIIT burns in a session
The evidence supports the idea that HIIT is high-intensity and burns calories both during and after exercise, but it does not provide a precise, universally applicable number of calories burned per session for weight loss. ## How HIIT compares to steady-state cardio for weight loss
The evidence indicates that HIIT may offer some advantages over steady-state cardio, but the weight-loss comparison is not straightforward. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that aerobic exercise at least 150 minutes per week was associated with clinically important reductions in waist circumference and measures of body fat [N2-R1]. Another study on high-intensity intermittent exercise and fat loss notes that brief HIIE interventions (2 to 6 weeks) only resulted in negligible weight loss, suggesting that duration and program design matter [N2-R2]. A comparative study of HIIT versus moderate continuous training found both methods had positive effects on aerobic capacity, fat oxidation, and other metabolic outcomes [N2-R3]. Overall, HIIT appears to be a time-efficient and metabolically stimulating option, but steady-state cardio may still have a more consistent and reproducible weight-loss effect in many people [N2-R1][N2-F3].

The evidence is clear that exercise alone is unlikely to produce substantial weight loss without dietary changes. The nutrition and lifestyle search results emphasize that small, balanced meals throughout the day help keep energy levels steady, and that nutrition supports sleep and exercise [N5-R1]. In short, the evidence supports the view that total energy deficit—driven by diet and expenditure—is the dominant determinant of weight loss, while HIIT contributes more through metabolic stimulation, time efficiency, and adaptation than through massive calorie burning alone [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

HIIT can realistically support weight loss by improving metabolism, burning calories during and after exercise, and offering a time-efficient way to accumulate physical activity [N1-R2][N4-F4]. Diet and total energy deficit remain far more important than exercise alone; without dietary changes and an overall energy deficit, even intense HIIT is unlikely to produce rapid, meaningful weight loss [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

- **After workouts**: Post-workout nutrition should support recovery and muscle repair, with protein and carbohydrates likely important [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]

---

## 4) Bottom line: What the patient should understand

If the goal is **to lose weight extremely fast using maximum intensity**, the evidence supports a **qualified “yes”**: HIIT can help, but only when combined with diet, recovery, and sensible training limits [N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2]. However, the evidence also clearly shows that:
- **HIIT is not superior to steady-state cardio in all weight-loss contexts** [N2-F3]
- **Diet and total energy deficit matter far more than exercise alone** [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]
- **Extreme daily high-intensity training is not safe or realistic** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]
- **Recovery, sleep, and gradual progression are essential** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2]

## Practical recommendation
A realistic daily plan should be:
1. **Balanced and progressive**—HIIT, cardio, strength training, and rest [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R4]
2. **Not all-out every day**—include rest days and adjust intensity gradually [N3-R2][N6-R2]
3. **Supported by nutrition and sleep**—balanced meals, hydration, and good sleep [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5]
4. **Designed for weight loss, not just intensity**—prioritize total energy deficit and sustainable training [N2-R1][N2-F3][N5-R1][N5-R3]

## Final advice
If the patient wants to “lose weight extremely fast,” the evidence suggests that **maximum intensity alone is not the best path**. The safest, most realistic, and most effective approach is to combine HIIT with diet, recovery, sleep, and a gradual, sustainable training plan [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-F3][N3-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N6-R1].
